# Datatypes

Datatypes are values, not instances. Constructors and constants are reached
through the type's name and are camelCase (`CFrame.new`, `CFrame.identity`).
Members reached through a value are PascalCase (`v.Magnitude`,
`cf:Inverse()`).

## AnimationTrack

One clip playing on one `AnimationPlayer`, returned by `LoadAnimation`. It is a handle, not an instance: it has no parent and is not in the tree. Its properties can be set, and every holder of the handle sees the change.

A track runs on simulation time, scaled by `Speed`, so a clip is at the same position on the same tick in a replay as it was live.

## AnimationTrack — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Ended` | `Signal<>` | — | read-only | A signal that fires on the tick a track that is not `Looped` reaches the end of its clip. `Stop` does not fire it, so code that starts the next animation from this signal is not triggered by an interrupted one. |
| `Length` | `number` | — | read-only | The duration of the clip, in seconds, or 0 if the clip was not found. |
| `Looped` | `boolean` | — | read/write | Whether the track starts again when it reaches the end of its clip. A looped track never fires `Ended`. |
| `Playing` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether the track is advancing. It becomes false when a track that is not `Looped` reaches the end of its clip. Such a track keeps showing its last frame until it is stopped or played again. |
| `Speed` | `number` | — | read/write | How fast the clip plays. 2 is twice as fast and half as long. 0 holds the current pose. |
| `TimePosition` | `number` | — | read-only | The current position in the clip, in seconds. |
| `Weight` | `number` | — | read/write | How much this track contributes when several tracks animate the same skeleton. Setting it takes effect immediately; to fade a track in or out, pass a fade time to `Play` or `Stop`.<br><br>Tracks are blended as a weighted average for each joint. A joint that no playing clip animates keeps its rest pose. |

## AnimationTrack — methods

### `Play(fadeTime: number?)`

Plays the clip from the beginning, every time it is called, so an animation triggered twice plays twice.

`fadeTime` fades the track's weight in from 0 to its `Weight` over that many seconds, which blends it smoothly with what is already playing.

### `Stop(fadeTime: number?)`

Stops the track. With `fadeTime`, its weight fades out over that many seconds and the track stops when the weight reaches 0. Without it, the track stops immediately. `Ended` does not fire in either case.

## CFrame

A position and an orientation: a rotation plus a translation. Use it to place and orient anything in the world.

The translation is stored in 64-bit floats, so a `CFrame` stays precise far from the origin. `Position` is that translation rounded to 32 bits. In a very large world, compute with `CFrame` values instead of converting to positions and back.

The world is right-handed, with Y up and -Z forward, as in glTF.

`CFrame * CFrame` combines two transforms. `CFrame * vector` transforms a point, including the translation. `==` compares every component exactly.

## CFrame — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `identity` | `CFrame` | — | read-only | The `CFrame` at the origin with no rotation. `cf * CFrame.identity == cf`. |

## CFrame — constructors

### `fromAxisAngle(axis: vector, angle: number): CFrame`

Returns a rotation of `angle` radians about `axis`, by the right-hand rule, at the origin. The length of the axis is ignored.

### `fromEuler(rx: number, ry: number, rz: number, order: Enum.RotationOrder? = Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ): CFrame`

Returns a rotation from three angles, in radians, applied in the order that `order` gives. Each rotation is about the axes produced by the previous one (intrinsic rotations), and positive angles follow the right-hand rule.

### `fromMatrix(position: vector, right: vector, up: vector, back: vector): CFrame`

Returns a `CFrame` from a position and three axes. The third axis is the back direction, so `LookVector` is `-back`. The axes are stored as given, even if they are not unit length or not perpendicular; call `Orthonormalize` to correct them.

### `fromQuaternion(position: vector, qx: number, qy: number, qz: number, qw: number): CFrame`

Returns a `CFrame` at `position` with the rotation of the quaternion `(qx, qy, qz, qw)`, with w last. The quaternion is normalized.

### `lookAt(position: vector, target: vector, up: vector? = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)): CFrame`

Returns a `CFrame` at `position` whose `LookVector` points toward `target`. `up` sets which way is up and defaults to `(0, 1, 0)`. If `target` equals `position`, or `up` is parallel to the direction, the result has no rotation.

### `new(position: vector): CFrame`

Returns a `CFrame` at `position` with no rotation. A vector has 32-bit components; pass three numbers where the extra precision matters.

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0, z: number? = 0): CFrame`

Returns a `CFrame` at the given position with no rotation. A missing component is 0, so `CFrame.new()` is the identity. The components are stored as 64-bit floats.

## CFrame — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `LookVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The forward direction, which is the -Z axis. Because forward is -Z, `RightVector:Cross(UpVector)` is `-LookVector`. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | The translation, as a vector. The value is rounded from 64 to 32 bits, so it loses precision far from the origin. |
| `RightVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The direction of the +X axis. |
| `Rotation` | `CFrame` | — | read-only | The same orientation with the translation set to zero. |
| `UpVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The direction of the +Y axis. |

## CFrame — methods

### `Inverse(): CFrame`

Returns the transform that reverses this one: `cf * cf:Inverse()` is the identity, up to rounding.

### `Lerp(goal: CFrame, alpha: number): CFrame`

Returns the interpolation toward `goal`. The position is interpolated linearly and the rotation spherically, so the rotation turns at a constant rate. `alpha` is not clamped, so a value outside 0 to 1 extrapolates.

### `Orthonormalize(): CFrame`

Returns the `CFrame` with its axes made unit length and perpendicular, and its position unchanged. `LookVector` keeps its direction, `UpVector` is made perpendicular to it, and `RightVector` follows from the two. Use it on a `CFrame` built with `fromMatrix`, or after many multiplications have accumulated rounding error.

### `PointToObjectSpace(point: vector): vector`

Converts a world-space position to this `CFrame`'s local space. It returns `self:Inverse() * point`.

### `PointToWorldSpace(point: vector): vector`

Converts a position from this `CFrame`'s local space to world space. It returns `self * point`.

### `ToAxisAngle(): (vector, number)`

Returns the rotation as a unit axis and an angle in radians. It is the inverse of `fromAxisAngle`.

### `ToEuler(order: Enum.RotationOrder? = Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ): (number, number, number)`

Returns the rotation as three angles `(rx, ry, rz)`, in radians, in the parameter order of `fromEuler`. It is the inverse of `fromEuler` for the same `order`. Euler angles are not unique, so converting to angles and back gives an equivalent rotation, not necessarily the same three numbers.

### `ToObjectSpace(cf: CFrame): CFrame`

Converts the world-space `cf` to this `CFrame`'s local space. It returns `self:Inverse() * cf`.

### `ToQuaternion(): (number, number, number, number)`

Returns the rotation as a quaternion `(qx, qy, qz, qw)`, with w last. It is the inverse of `fromQuaternion`.

### `ToWorldSpace(cf: CFrame): CFrame`

Converts `cf` from this `CFrame`'s local space to world space. It returns `self * cf`.

### `VectorToObjectSpace(direction: vector): vector`

Converts a world-space direction to this `CFrame`'s local space, applying the rotation only. It returns `self.Rotation:Inverse() * direction`.

### `VectorToWorldSpace(direction: vector): vector`

Converts a direction from this `CFrame`'s local space to world space, applying the rotation only. It returns `self.Rotation * direction`. Use it for directions such as surface normals; `PointToWorldSpace` would also add the position.

## CFrame — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__mul` | `(other: CFrame): CFrame` | Combines two transforms. `a * b` applies `b` first and then `a`. |
| `__mul` | `(point: vector): vector` | Transforms a point, including the translation. For a direction, use `VectorToWorldSpace`. |
| `__eq` | `(other: CFrame): boolean` | Compares two `CFrame` values exactly, component by component, with no tolerance. |

## Collector

Collects things to clean up together, such as connections, instances, threads and functions. `Cleanup` cleans each one in the way its type requires, newest first.

## Collector — constructors

### `new(): Collector`

Returns a new, empty `Collector`.

## Collector — methods

### `Add(object: any, method: (string | boolean)? = nil, key: any? = nil): any`

Adds `object` to be cleaned up later, and returns it. How it is cleaned depends on its type: a function is called, a thread is canceled, a `Connection` is disconnected, a `Promise` is canceled, and an `Instance`, a `Signal` or any object with a `Destroy` method is destroyed.

`method` names a method to call instead, or true to call the object itself. `key` gives the object a name for `Remove` and `Get`. Adding under a key that is already in use cleans the object that was there first.

### `AddPromise(promise: Promise): Promise`

Adds a promise to be canceled on cleanup, and returns it. If the promise settles by itself first, it is removed from the collector.

### `Cleanup()`

Cleans every object, newest first. The collector stays usable afterward.

### `Destroy()`

Cleans every object. Adding to the collector afterward raises an error.

### `Get(key: any): any`

Returns the object stored under `key`, or nil.

### `LinkToInstance(instance: Instance, allowMultiple: boolean? = nil): Connection`

Cleans the collector when `instance` is destroyed, and returns the connection that does so. A new link replaces the previous one unless `allowMultiple` is true.

### `Remove(key: any)`

Cleans the object stored under `key` immediately and removes it from the collector.

### `RemoveNoClean(key: any)`

Removes the object stored under `key` from the collector without cleaning it.

## Color3

A color with red, green and blue channels, each a 32-bit float nominally from 0 to 1. The channels are not clamped: values above 1 are valid and are used for bright emissive colors and tints. `==` compares every channel exactly.

## Color3 — constructors

### `fromHSV(h: number, s: number, v: number): Color3`

Returns a color from hue, saturation and value, each from 0 to 1. The hue is also 0 to 1, not degrees: `fromHSV(1/3, 1, 1)` is green.

### `fromHex(hex: string): Color3`

Returns a color from a hexadecimal string. It accepts `#rrggbb`, `rrggbb`, `#rgb` and `rgb`, in upper or lower case. Raises an error for any other string.

### `fromRGB(r: number, g: number, b: number): Color3`

Returns a color from three channels in the range 0 to 255, as color pickers show them. Each channel is divided by 255.

### `new(r: number? = 0, g: number? = 0, b: number? = 0): Color3`

Returns a color from three channels in the range 0 to 1. Each defaults to 0, so `Color3.new()` is black. Values outside the range are kept.

## Color3 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `B` | `number` | — | read-only | The blue channel, nominally 0 to 1 and not clamped. |
| `G` | `number` | — | read-only | The green channel, nominally 0 to 1 and not clamped. |
| `R` | `number` | — | read-only | The red channel, nominally 0 to 1 and not clamped. |

## Color3 — methods

### `Lerp(goal: Color3, alpha: number): Color3`

Returns the linear interpolation toward `goal`, channel by channel in RGB. `alpha` is not clamped.

### `ToHSV(): (number, number, number)`

Returns the color as hue, saturation and value, each from 0 to 1. It is the inverse of `fromHSV`. The hue of a gray is 0.

### `ToHex(): string`

Returns the color as six lowercase hexadecimal digits with no leading `#`, such as `"ff8800"`. Each channel is clamped to the range 0 to 255, so a channel above 1 is not preserved.

## Color3 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: Color3): boolean` | Compares two colors exactly, channel by channel. Two colors that would look the same after clamping are still unequal if their stored values differ. |

## ColorSequence

A gradient of colors over the range 0 to 1, made of 2 to 20 stops. The first stop is at 0 and the last at 1, and the color between two stops is interpolated linearly. `UIGradient.Color` is one. It is immutable, and `==` compares every stop.

## ColorSequence — constructors

### `new(color: Color3): ColorSequence`

Returns a sequence of one color from start to end.

### `new(from: Color3, to: Color3): ColorSequence`

Returns a sequence that blends from `from` at 0 to `to` at 1.

### `new(keypoints: { ColorSequenceKeypoint }): ColorSequence`

Returns a sequence from a list of 2 to 20 stops. Their times must increase, the first must be exactly 0, and the last exactly 1. Two stops at the same time make a hard edge. Raises an error for any other list.

## ColorSequence — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Keypoints` | `{ ColorSequenceKeypoint }` | — | read-only | The stops, in order of time. Each read returns a new table. |

## ColorSequence — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: ColorSequence): boolean` | Compares every stop exactly. |

## ColorSequenceKeypoint

One stop of a `ColorSequence`: a color at a time from 0 to 1. It is immutable, and `==` compares exactly.

## ColorSequenceKeypoint — constructors

### `new(time: number, color: Color3): ColorSequenceKeypoint`

Returns a stop at `time`, which must be from 0 to 1.

## ColorSequenceKeypoint — properties

| `Time` | `number` | — | read-only | The position of the stop along the sequence, from 0 to 1. |
| `Value` | `Color3` | — | read-only | The color at that position. |

## Connection

The handle that `Signal:Connect` and `Signal:Once` return. Use it to disconnect the handler. It cannot be created directly.

## Connection — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Connected` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether the handler is still connected. It is false after `Disconnect`, after the signal is destroyed, and after a `Once` handler has run. |

## Connection — methods

### `Disconnect()`

Disconnects the handler. Calling it again does nothing. A fire that was queued before the call can still run the handler once.

## DataRecord

A player's record in an online game's database, returned by `DataService:LoadAsync` and held by this world. It holds values under string keys, as a `SaveSlot` does, and raises the same errors for a value it cannot hold. Once it is let go, by `Release` or as its player leaves, every member but `Released` raises an error.

## DataRecord — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Released` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether this world has let the record go. |

## DataRecord — methods

### `Get(key: string): any`

Returns a copy of the value stored under `key`, or nil.

### `GetKeys(): { string }`

Returns every key, sorted.

### `Release()`

Writes the record and lets it go, so another world can load it. Doing it again does nothing.

### `Remove(key: string)`

Removes `key` and its value.

### `Save()`

Writes the record now, without waiting for the next write behind. It does not wait for the database.

### `Set(key: string, value: any)`

Stores a copy of `value` under `key`. A value of nil removes the key. Raises an error for a value that cannot be saved, and for one that would make the record larger than 4 MB.

### `Update(key: string, transform: (any) -> any): any`

Calls `transform` with the value stored under `key`, stores what it returns, and returns that value. The function must not yield.

## InputObject

One input, as passed by `InputService.InputBegan`, `InputChanged` and `InputEnded`. It is a read-only snapshot of what happened on one tick, not a live object.

These events are raised by the engine on simulation ticks, after the interface has consumed what it uses. In a replay they come from the recorded input, so a replay reproduces every input a game reads.

## InputObject — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Delta` | `vector` | — | read-only | How much the input moved since the last tick, in the same units as `Position`. `z` is the movement of the mouse wheel. It is zero for an input that is not a movement. |
| `GamepadId` | `number` | — | read-only | The id of the gamepad that produced the input. Presses on different gamepads at the same time keep their own ids. It is 0 for other devices. A gamepad that reconnects can get a new id. |
| `KeyCode` | `Enum.KeyCode` | — | read-only | The key, button or axis. It is `Unknown` for pointer movement and the mouse wheel, which are not keys. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | The position of the pointer, in window pixels measured from the top left, with the accumulated wheel movement in `z`. For a gamepad axis it is the position of the axis instead: `x` and `y` for a stick, and `x` for a trigger. |
| `TouchId` | `number` | — | read-only | The finger of a `Touch` input. The number is the same from the finger's `InputBegan` to its `InputEnded`, so a handler can follow several fingers at once. Numbers start at 1 and are reused after a finger lifts. It is 0 for an input that is not a touch. |
| `UserInputType` | `Enum.UserInputType` | — | read-only | The kind of input, for a handler that does not need to know which key it was. |

## IntentWriter

The object a function bound with `RunService:BindToIntent` uses to set the current tick's intents. It is valid only during that call.

## IntentWriter — methods

### `Set(action: string, value: boolean | number | Vector2 | vector)`

Sets the current tick's intent named `action`. A boolean is a button that is pressed or not, a number is one axis, a `Vector2` is two axes and a `vector` is three. Raises an error for a value that is not finite.

## Material

The appearance of a surface: its color, its texture maps, and how rough and metallic it is. It also sets how the surface behaves in physics and what tags it has. A material is not an instance. A project stores each material as a `.material.json` file under `content/`, and a part uses one through `BasePart.Material`.

There are two kinds of material handle. `Material.load` returns the shared handle of a material file, which is read-only: setting a property on it raises an error, because the change would affect every part that uses the file. `Clone` returns a copy that exists only at run time, can be changed, and is never saved.

Nothing is cloned automatically. Reading `part.Material` returns the handle the part uses, and changing a clone changes every part that uses that clone.

## Material — constructors

### `load(content: Content): Material`

Returns the shared, read-only handle of a material file, as in `Material.load("asset://materials/brick.material.json")`. Raises an error if the path is not a material.

## Material — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `AlphaCutoff` | `number` | — | read/write | The alpha threshold for `Mask` mode. It is used only in that mode. |
| `AlphaMode` | `Enum.AlphaMode` | — | read/write | How the alpha of the base color is used. `Opaque` ignores it, `Mask` draws only the pixels whose alpha is at least `AlphaCutoff`, and `Blend` blends the surface with what is behind it. |
| `BlendSharpness` | `number` | — | read/write | How sharp the edge is where this terrain layer meets another, from 0 (a wide fade) to 1 (a sharp line that follows the height map). Only terrain uses it. |
| `Color` | `Color3` | — | read/write | The base color of the surface. It is multiplied by `ColorMap` if there is one. |
| `ColorMap` | `Content` | — | read/write | The base color image, multiplied by `Color`. It holds color data in sRGB, unlike the normal and metallic-roughness maps, which hold linear data. |
| `DoubleSided` | `boolean` | — | read/write | Whether back faces are drawn. Turn it on for thin surfaces such as leaves and cloth. |
| `Emissive` | `Color3` | — | read/write | The color of the light the surface gives off by itself. It makes the surface bright but does not light other objects; use a `PointLight` for that. |
| `EmissiveMap` | `Content` | — | read/write | An image of the light the surface gives off, multiplied by `Emissive`. It holds color data. |
| `FootstepSound` | `Content` | — | read/write | The sound of a footstep on this surface, as a content path, or an empty string. The engine does not play it; a game reads it through `CharacterBody.FloorMaterial` and plays it in time with the character's steps. |
| `Friction` | `number` | — | read/write | How much a body that touches this surface resists sliding. A part uses its material's friction unless the part's own `Friction` is set, and terrain uses the friction of the material drawn at each point. The default is 0.3. |
| `HeightMap` | `string` | — | read/write | A height image for a terrain layer, in which white is high. Where two layers meet, the higher one shows through. Only terrain uses it. |
| `HexTiling` | `boolean` | — | read/write | Whether a terrain layer's textures are placed in hexagonal cells, each randomly offset and rotated, with blended borders. It hides repetition, which shows most in photographic textures. It samples each texture three times instead of once. Off by default. Only terrain uses it. |
| `MetallicRoughnessMap` | `Content` | — | read/write | An image with occlusion in its red channel, roughness in green and metalness in blue, as in glTF. It holds linear data, not color. |
| `Metalness` | `number` | — | read/write | How metallic the surface is, from 0 (not a metal, such as plastic, stone or wood) to 1 (bare metal). |
| `NormalMap` | `Content` | — | read/write | A normal map in tangent space. It holds linear data, not color. |
| `NormalScale` | `number` | — | read/write | The strength of the normal map. 1 uses the map as authored, and 0 gives a flat surface. |
| `Restitution` | `number` | — | read/write | The fraction of its speed a body keeps when it bounces off this surface, from 0 (no bounce) to 1. The default is 0. |
| `Roughness` | `number` | — | read/write | How rough the surface is, from 0 (a mirror) to 1 (fully matte). The default is 0.7. |
| `Source` | `Content` | — | read-only | The path of the material file this handle comes from. For a clone, including a clone of a clone, it is the file the original was loaded from. |
| `Tags` | `{ string }` | — | read/write | Labels a game can read from a surface, such as "slippery", "metal" or "lava", in the order the material lists them. Each read returns a new table. |
| `TileSize` | `number` | — | read/write | The size of one repeat of the textures on a part's faces, in meters. A face shows as many repeats as fit along it, so the texture has the same scale on every face of a part. At 0, each texture is stretched over the whole face. A `MeshPart` uses the UVs from its file instead. A terrain layer also repeats at this size. |
| `TilingFarScale` | `number` | — | read/write | The scale of a second, larger sample of a terrain layer's textures that is blended in with distance, from 1 (none) to 32. The default is 6. Only terrain uses it. |
| `TilingVariation` | `number` | — | read/write | How much a large-scale pattern, tens of meters across, varies the color of a terrain layer, from 0 (none) to 1. It hides the repetition of the texture. The default is 0.5. Only terrain uses it. |
| `Transparency` | `number` | — | read/write | How transparent the surface is, from 0 (opaque) to 1 (invisible). |
| `Triplanar` | `boolean` | — | read/write | Whether a terrain layer's textures are projected along three axes, so that they do not stretch on a cliff. On by default. Only terrain uses it. |

## Material — methods

### `Clone(): Material`

Returns a copy of the material that can be changed. The copy has the same properties and the same `Source`, exists only at run time and is never saved. Assign it with `part.Material = copy` and then change it: every part that uses the copy changes, and nothing else does.

### `GetShaderParameter(name: string): (number | Vector2 | vector | { number } | string)?`

Returns the value this material sets for a parameter of its surface shader, or nil if it leaves the parameter at the shader's default. The value is a number, a `Vector2`, a `vector` (also used for a color), a table of four numbers, or the path of a texture.

### `SetShaderParameter(name: string, value: number | boolean | Vector2 | vector | Color3 | { number } | string)`

Sets a parameter of the material's surface shader. It works only on a clone, because a loaded material is shared and read-only. A string value is the path of a texture. Every part that uses the clone is drawn with the new value from the next frame. The value is not replicated: set it on the machine that draws the part.

## NumberSequence

A series of numbers over the range 0 to 1, made of 2 to 20 stops. The first stop is at 0 and the last at 1, and the value between two stops is interpolated linearly. `UIGradient.Transparency` is one. It is immutable, and `==` compares every stop.

Returns a sequence of one number from start to end.

### `new(from: number, to: number): NumberSequence`

Returns a sequence that blends from `from` at 0 to `to` at 1.

### `new(keypoints: { NumberSequenceKeypoint }): NumberSequence`

Returns a sequence from a list of 2 to 20 stops. Their times must increase, the first must be exactly 0, and the last exactly 1. Raises an error for any other list.

## PredictedStep

One tick of one character, passed to a function bound with `RunService:BindToPredictedStep` or `BasePart:BindToPredictedTouch`. It is valid only during that call.

## PredictedStep — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Character` | `BasePart` | — | read-only | The character being simulated: the `Character` of its player on this machine. |
| `DeltaTime` | `number` | — | read-only | The length of the step, in seconds. |
| `Player` | `Player` | — | read-only | The player the character belongs to. |
| `Random` | `Random` | — | read-only | A random number generator seeded from the player and `Tick`. It gives the same numbers when the step is first simulated and when it is replayed, on the client and on the authority. Each read returns a generator at the start of its sequence, so store it in a local variable. |
| `Replaying` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether this step is being simulated again after a correction, on a client. Check it before doing something that must happen only once, such as playing a sound or emitting particles. |
| `Tick` | `number` | — | read-only | The player's own tick number: the number their machine gave to the tick of input this step uses. It is the same on the authority and on the player's client, so use it to time an effect such as a dash that lasts twenty ticks. |

## PredictedStep — methods

### `GetIntent(action: string): boolean | number | Vector2 | vector`

Returns the player's intent named `action` for this tick, as `Player:GetIntent` does. In a replayed step, it returns the value the tick originally had.

### `Pressed(action: string): boolean`

Returns whether the button `action` was pressed on this tick: it is held now and was not held on the previous step.

## Promise

A value that becomes available later. A promise is resolved with values or rejected with an error, and code attaches handlers for either outcome.

The executor of a new promise runs immediately, in its own thread. Resolving a promise with another promise adopts that promise's outcome. A handler that raises an error rejects the promise it feeds. Canceling a promise cancels every promise that depends on it. A rejection that no handler receives is reported as a warning. Delays and timeouts use simulation time.

## Promise — constructors

### `all(promises: { Promise }): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves with every value, in order, when all the promises resolve. It rejects with the first rejection and cancels the others.

### `allSettled(promises: { Promise }): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves when every promise has settled, with the final status of each.

### `any(promises: { Promise }): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves with the value of the first promise to resolve. It rejects if all of them reject.

### `defer(executor: (resolve: (...any) -> (), reject: (...any) -> (), onCancel: (hook: (() -> ())?) -> boolean) -> ()): Promise`

Returns a promise like `new`, except that the executor runs at the next resumption point instead of immediately.

### `delay(seconds: number): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves after `seconds` of simulation time, with `seconds` as its value.

### `fromEvent(event: Signal<...any>, predicate: ((...any) -> boolean)? = nil): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves with the arguments of the next fire of a signal that `predicate` accepts, and then disconnects from the signal.

### `is(value: any): boolean`

Returns whether `value` is a `Promise`.

### `new(executor: (resolve: (...any) -> (), reject: (...any) -> (), onCancel: (hook: (() -> ())?) -> boolean) -> ()): Promise`

Returns a promise that runs `executor(resolve, reject, onCancel)` immediately, in its own thread.

### `promisify(fn: (...any) -> ...any): (...any) -> Promise`

Returns a function that calls `fn` and returns a promise for its result.

### `race(promises: { Promise }): Promise`

Returns a promise that settles the way the first of the promises to settle does, and cancels the others.

### `reject(values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise that is already rejected with the given values.

### `resolve(values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise that is already resolved with the given values.

### `retry(fn: (...any) -> ...any, times: number, values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise for `fn(...)`, like `try`, that calls the function again up to `times` more times while it rejects.

### `retryWithDelay(fn: (...any) -> ...any, times: number, seconds: number, values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise like `retry`, with `seconds` of simulation time before each new attempt.

### `some(promises: { Promise }, count: number): Promise`

Returns a promise that resolves with the values of the first `count` promises to resolve. It rejects as soon as that many can no longer resolve.

### `try(fn: (...any) -> ...any, values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise for the call `fn(...)`. What the function returns resolves the promise, and an error it raises rejects it.

## Promise — methods

### `AndThen(onResolved: ((...any) -> ...any)? = nil, onRejected: ((...any) -> ...any)? = nil): Promise`

Returns a promise for the result of `onResolved`, or of `onRejected` if this promise rejects. A handler that raises an error rejects the new promise. If a handler returns a promise, the new promise waits for it.

### `AndThenCall(fn: (...any) -> ...any, values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise that, when this one resolves, calls `fn` with the given arguments instead of the resolved values.

### `AndThenReturn(values: ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise that, when this one resolves, resolves with the given values instead.

### `Await(): (boolean, ...any)`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Yields until the promise settles. Returns true and the resolved values, or false and the rejection. A canceled promise returns false.

### `AwaitStatus(): (EnumPromiseState, ...any)`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Yields until the promise settles, like `Await`, and returns the status in place of the boolean.

### `Cancel()`

Cancels the promise. The executor stops, its cancel hook runs, and every promise that depends on this one is canceled. The promise it depends on is also canceled once nothing else depends on it.

### `Catch(onRejected: (...any) -> ...any): Promise`

Returns a promise for the result of `onRejected` if this promise rejects. It is the same as `AndThen(nil, onRejected)`.

### `ExpectAsync(): ...any`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Yields until the promise settles and returns the resolved values. Raises an error with the rejection if the promise rejects.

### `Finally(fn: (status: EnumPromiseState) -> ...any): Promise`

Calls `fn` with the final status when this promise settles in any way. Returns a promise that settles the way this one did.

### `GetStatus(): EnumPromiseState`

Returns the status of the promise: `Enum.PromiseState.Started`, `Resolved`, `Rejected` or `Canceled`.

### `Now(rejection: any? = nil): Promise`

Returns a promise that passes this one's values on if it is already resolved, and otherwise rejects immediately with `rejection`.

### `Tap(fn: (...any) -> ...any): Promise`

Calls `fn` with the resolved values and returns a promise that resolves with those same values, whatever `fn` returns.

### `Timeout(seconds: number, rejection: any? = nil): Promise`

Returns a promise that rejects with `rejection` if this one does not settle within `seconds` of simulation time. This promise is canceled when the time runs out.

## Random

A seeded pseudorandom number generator. Use it for every random number in simulation code. The same seed gives the same sequence on the same engine build and platform, which is what makes a replay reproduce a run: a replay stores seeds, not results.

## Random — constructors

### `new(seed: number? = nil): Random`

Returns a generator seeded with `seed`, truncated to an integer. With no seed, a seed is taken from the system and the sequence is different on every run. Do not use an unseeded generator in simulation code; `ludwerk check` reports it. Use one only for effects that do not affect gameplay.

## Random — methods

### `Clone(): Random`

Returns a copy of the generator at the same point in its sequence. The copy and the original then continue independently. Use it to give a subsystem its own deterministic stream.

### `NextInteger(min: number, max: number): number`

Returns the next integer from `min` to `max`, both included. Raises an error if `min` is greater than `max`, or if either is not an integer.

### `NextNumber(min: number? = 0, max: number? = 1): number`

Returns the next number from `min` up to but not including `max`. The defaults are 0 and 1. Raises an error if `min` is greater than `max`.

### `NextUnitVector(): vector`

Returns a random direction of length 1, uniformly distributed over the sphere.

## RaycastParams

Sets what a raycast or other spatial query can hit. Every query on `Workspace` accepts one; without it, the query can hit everything that has `CanQuery` on. It is created from a table of options.

## RaycastParams — constructors

### `new(options: { Filter: { Instance }?, FilterType: Enum.RaycastFilterType?, CollisionGroup: string? }? = nil): RaycastParams`

Returns params from a table of options. `Filter` defaults to an empty list, `FilterType` to `Exclude` and `CollisionGroup` to an empty string, which means every group. An empty `Exclude` filter hits everything, and an empty `Include` filter hits nothing.

## RaycastParams — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CollisionGroup` | `string` | — | read-only | The collision group a hit must belong to, or an empty string for any group. Restricting a query to one group is cheaper than hitting everything and filtering the results. |
| `Filter` | `{ Instance }` | — | read-only | The instances the filter lists. Each read returns a new array. The descendants of a listed instance are included, so listing a `Model` covers its parts. |
| `FilterType` | `Enum.RaycastFilterType` | — | read-only | Whether `Filter` lists the only instances that can be hit (`Include`) or the instances to ignore (`Exclude`). |

## RaycastResult

The result of a raycast: what was hit and where. `Workspace:Raycast` and `Workspace:Spherecast` return one, or nil when nothing was hit.

## RaycastResult — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Distance` | `number` | — | read-only | The distance from the origin of the ray to the hit, in meters. |
| `Instance` | `BasePart` | — | read-only | The part that was hit. |
| `Material` | `Material?` | — | read-only | The material of the surface at the hit: the part's material, or nil if the part has none. On a `Terrain`, it is the layer drawn at that point, including painted materials and rules, so snow that a rule draws over rock above a certain height is reported as snow. Read its `Friction`, `FootstepSound` and `Tags` to choose a footstep, a skid or an impact effect. |
| `Normal` | `vector` | — | read-only | The surface normal at the hit, pointing out of the surface. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | The position of the hit, in world space. |

## RaycastResult2D

The result of `Workspace:Raycast2D`: what was hit on the 2D plane and where. The method returns nil when nothing was hit.

## RaycastResult2D — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Distance` | `number` | — | read-only | The distance from the origin of the ray to the hit, in meters. |
| `Instance` | `Instance` | — | read-only | The `Part2D` or `Tilemap2D` that was hit. |
| `Normal` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The surface normal at the hit, pointing out of the surface. |
| `Position` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The position of the hit, in meters on the 2D plane. |

## Rect

A rectangle on screen, given by two corners in pixels. The corners are not sorted or checked, so a rectangle can be inverted.

## Rect — constructors

### `new(min: Vector2, max: Vector2): Rect`

Returns a rectangle from its two corners.

## Rect — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Height` | `number` | — | read-only | The height, `Max.Y - Min.Y`. It is negative for an inverted rectangle. |
| `Max` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The second corner. |
| `Min` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The first corner. |
| `Width` | `number` | — | read-only | The width, `Max.X - Min.X`. It is negative for an inverted rectangle. |

## Rect — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: Rect): boolean` | Compares both corners exactly. |

## SaveSlot

One named save of a game, returned by `SaveService:GetSlotAsync`. It holds values under string keys.

A value can be anything an attribute can hold: a string, a number, a boolean, a vector, a `CFrame`, a `Color3`, a `Vector2`, a `UDim`, a `UDim2`, a `Rect` or a sequence. It can also be a table of such values, nested, with string keys or array indices. `Set` raises an error for a function, a thread, an instance or a table that contains itself.

Changes are written to disk automatically: at most once per second while something has changed, when the game closes, and when the app goes to the background, because a phone can close a game in the background without warning. `SaveAsync` writes immediately and waits. `Get` returns a copy; changing the copy changes nothing until it is passed to `Set`.

## SaveSlot — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Changed` | `Signal<string>` | — | read-only | A signal that fires when `Set`, `Update` or `Remove` changes a key. Passes the key. |
| `Name` | `string` | — | read-only | The name of the slot. |
| `Recovered` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether the slot's data was read successfully. It is false when the slot's file and its backup were both damaged and the slot started empty, so that the game can tell the player. It is true otherwise, including for a slot that did not exist yet. |

## SaveSlot — methods

### `Get(key: string): any`

Returns a copy of the value stored under `key`, or nil.

### `GetKeys(): { string }`

Returns every key, sorted.

### `Remove(key: string)`

Removes `key` and its value.

### `SaveAsync()`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Writes the slot to disk immediately and yields until it is written. Raises an error if the write fails.

### `Set(key: string, value: any)`

Stores a copy of `value` under `key`. A value of nil removes the key. Raises an error for a value that cannot be saved, and for a value that would make the slot larger than the project's `[save] max_slot_bytes`.

### `Update(key: string, transform: (any) -> any): any`

Calls `transform` with the value stored under `key`, stores what it returns, and returns that value. The function must not yield.

## Scene

A scene of the game, such as a level, a menu or an arena. A scene stays open until `SceneService:LoadScene` changes to another.

The global `scene` is available in every script, like `game`, and always refers to the scene that is open when it is read. `SceneService.CurrentScene` returns the same scene as an object that keeps referring to that scene.

A `Scene` object kept after its scene closes is closed: `IsOpen` returns false, `BindToClose` and `BindToMessage` raise an error, and a message sent to it is dropped. Inside a `SubWorld`, `scene` is the sub-world's scene.

## Scene — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Name` | `string` | — | read-only | The name of the scene file without its folder or the `.scene.json` extension: `arena` for `scenes/arena.scene.json`. It is empty for a world that no scene file created. |
| `Path` | `string` | — | read-only | The path of the scene file relative to the content folder, such as `scenes/arena.scene.json`. |

## Scene — methods

### `BindToClose(callback: () -> ())`

Registers a function to run when this scene closes: when `LoadScene` changes to another scene, or when the game closes while this scene is open. Use it for what belongs to a level, such as saving its progress. Raises an error on a scene that has closed.

The scene change waits for the functions. Each runs in its own thread and can yield, for example in `SaveSlot:SaveAsync`, for up to the project's `[scene] close_grace_seconds` (5 by default). Then saves are written and the scene closes. Functions run in the order they were registered, and an error in one does not stop the others.

`game:BindToClose` is for the whole game. A function that a scene's script registers there is dropped when its scene closes, with a warning in the editor.

### `BindToMessage(topic: string, callback: (...any) -> ())`

Binds a function that runs with a message's values each time a message is sent to this scene under `topic`. The binding belongs to the script that made it and is removed with that script's scene. A message with no bound function is dropped, with a warning in the editor. Raises an error on a scene that has closed.

### `IsOpen(): boolean`

Returns whether this scene is the one that is open. It is false after the scene has closed, and for a scene that is still being prepared (see `SceneLoad.Scene`) until it opens. `scene:IsOpen()` is always true.

### `SendMessage(topic: string, arguments: ...any)`

Sends a message to this scene: every function bound to `topic` on it with `BindToMessage` runs with the message's values. The functions run deferred, in the order the messages were sent, each in its own thread. For example, a global script can tell the level `scene:SendMessage("OpenGate", "north")`.

Values arrive the way an attribute or a save stores them: a table as a copy without its metatable, a `buffer` as a copy, and an instance as the same instance. Raises an error that names the place for a function, a thread, a table that contains itself, or a live object such as a `Signal`, a `Connection` or a `Tween`.

A message to a closed scene is dropped. A message to a scene that is still being prepared waits until its scripts have started. Messages never leave this machine; to send between machines, use a `RemoteEvent`.

## SceneLoad

A scene that is being prepared while the current scene keeps running, returned by `SceneService:LoadSceneAsync`. Its file is read and parsed on another thread, and the meshes it uses are loaded.

The switch happens when the game calls `Activate`, or immediately for a load started with `Activate = true`. It happens between two ticks, like `LoadScene`: `SceneLoading` fires, the old scene's `scene:BindToClose` functions run and are waited for, and the prepared scene opens.

Only one load runs at a time: another `LoadSceneAsync` or a `LoadScene` cancels this one.

## SceneLoad — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Error` | `string?` | — | read-only | The reason the load failed, when `Status` is `Failed`. It is nil otherwise. |
| `Finished` | `Signal<boolean>` | — | read-only | A signal that fires once, when the load ends. Passes true if the scene opened, and false if the load failed or was canceled. |
| `Path` | `string` | — | read-only | The path of the scene file relative to the content folder. |
| `Progress` | `number` | — | read-only | The progress of the load, from 0 to 1. It never decreases. The first half is reading and parsing the file, and the second half is loading the meshes. It is 1 when `Ready` fires. |
| `Ready` | `Signal<>` | — | read-only | A signal that fires once, when the scene is prepared and waiting to be activated. |
| `Scene` | `Scene` | — | read-only | The scene that is being prepared. A message sent to it waits until the scene opens and its scripts have started, and is delivered before `SceneLoaded` fires. |
| `Status` | `Enum.SceneLoadStatus` | — | read-only | The stage of the load: `Preparing`, `Ready`, `Activating` and then `Done`, or `Failed` or `Canceled`. |

## SceneLoad — methods

### `Activate()`

Switches to the scene immediately if it is ready, or as soon as it is. Raises an error on a load that failed or was canceled.

### `Cancel()`

Discards the prepared scene. `Finished` fires with false. Does nothing after the switch has started.

## Signal

An event that handlers can connect to. Its type is written `Signal<T...>`, where `T...` is the list of values that handlers receive and `Wait` returns. A script creates its own with `Signal.new`.

Signals are deferred: firing one queues its handlers, and they run at the next resumption point, in the order the signals were fired. Within one fire, handlers run in the order they were connected.

Each handler runs in its own coroutine. An error in one handler does not stop the other handlers or the script that fired the signal.

## Signal — constructors

### `new(): Signal<T...>`

Returns a new signal owned by the script. The argument types are inferred from the calls to `Fire` and `Connect`; annotate the type, as in `Signal<string>` or `Signal<()>`, where they cannot be inferred.

## Signal — methods

### `Connect(handler: (T...) -> ()): Connection`

Connects `handler` to the signal and returns a `Connection` that disconnects it. The handlers of one fire run in the order they were connected. Do not rely on the order of handlers between different signals.

### `Destroy()`

Closes the signal. Fires that are already queued call no handlers, and every `Connection` reports `Connected` as false. Only a signal that a script created can be destroyed; an instance's signals are closed by `Instance:Destroy`.

### `DisconnectAll()`

Disconnects every handler and keeps the signal usable: it can be connected to and fired again. It works only on a signal that a script created, not on an instance's event.

### `Fire(values: T...)`

Queues a call to every connected handler with the given arguments. Nothing runs until the next resumption point. Tables are passed by reference, so a change made to one before the handlers run is visible to them.

### `Once(handler: (T...) -> ()): Connection`

Connects `handler` for one call only: it is disconnected as it is called. If the signal fires twice before the handlers run, the handler still runs once. A handler that raises an error is still disconnected.

### `Wait(): T...`

This method yields: the calling thread waits until it completes.

Yields the calling coroutine until the signal next fires, and returns the arguments of that fire. It counts as a connection made at the moment of the call, so it resumes in connection order among the handlers.

## Tween

A property animation, returned by `TweenService:Create`. It is a value, not an instance: it has no parent and is not in the tree.

A tween sets properties the way a script does. Each change fires `GetPropertyChangedSignal`, and a value that is out of range is refused, as for an assignment. It advances on simulation ticks, so it is reproducible.

A tween does not keep its instance alive. If the instance is destroyed, the tween stops and reports `Canceled`.

## Tween — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Completed` | `Signal<EnumPlaybackState>` | — | read-only | A signal that fires once when the tween ends. Passes the final state: `Completed` if the tween reached its end, or `Canceled` if it was stopped early. Check the state before acting on a finished animation. |
| `Instance` | `Instance?` | — | read-only | The instance the tween animates, or nil after that instance is destroyed. |
| `PlaybackState` | `Enum.PlaybackState` | — | read-only | The current state of the tween. |
| `TweenInfo` | `TweenInfo` | — | read-only | The `TweenInfo` the tween was created with. |

## Tween — methods

### `Cancel()`

Stops the tween before its end. The property keeps the value it had reached. `Completed` fires with `Canceled`.

### `Pause()`

Pauses the tween and leaves the property at its current value. `Play` resumes it.

### `Play()`

Starts the tween, or resumes a paused tween from where it stopped. Does nothing if the tween is already playing. To restart an animation, create a new tween.

## TweenInfo

Describes how a tween moves: its duration, its easing curve, how many times it repeats and its delay. It is immutable.

Times are in seconds of simulation time, the same seconds `task.wait` counts, so a tween lasts a whole number of ticks and a replay reproduces it exactly.

## TweenInfo — constructors

### `new(time: number? = 1, easingStyle: Enum.EasingStyle? = Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, easingDirection: Enum.EasingDirection? = Enum.EasingDirection.Out, repeatCount: number? = 0, reverses: boolean? = false, delayTime: number? = 0): TweenInfo`

Returns a `TweenInfo`. The defaults are one second, `Quad`, `Out`, no repeat, no reverse and no delay. Raises an error for a negative `time` or `delayTime`. A negative `repeatCount` repeats forever.

## TweenInfo — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DelayTime` | `number` | — | read-only | The time before the first pass and before each repeat, in seconds. During the delay, the property is not changed. |
| `EasingDirection` | `Enum.EasingDirection` | — | read-only | Which end of the pass the easing applies to. |
| `EasingStyle` | `Enum.EasingStyle` | — | read-only | The easing curve. |
| `RepeatCount` | `number` | — | read-only | The number of extra passes after the first. 0 plays once and 2 plays three times. A negative number repeats until the tween is canceled. |
| `Reverses` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether each pass is followed by the same pass backward. A reversing tween takes twice `Time` per repeat and ends where it started. |
| `Time` | `number` | — | read-only | The duration of one pass, in seconds, not counting the delay, the repeats or the return pass of a reversing tween. |

## TweenInfo — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: TweenInfo): boolean` | Compares two `TweenInfo` values exactly, field by field. |

## UDim

One axis of a UI position or size: a fraction of the parent (`Scale`) plus a number of pixels (`Offset`). "Half the parent minus eight pixels" is `UDim.new(0.5, -8)`, and it stays correct when the window is resized. It supports `+`, `-` and `==`.

## UDim — constructors

### `new(scale: number? = 0, offset: number? = 0): UDim`

Returns a `UDim` with the given scale and offset. Each defaults to 0.

## UDim — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Offset` | `number` | — | read-only | The number of pixels added after the scale is applied. |
| `Scale` | `number` | — | read-only | The fraction of the parent's size along the axis. 1 is the whole parent. It is not clamped, so values above 1 or below 0 are valid. |

## UDim — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: UDim): UDim` | Adds the scales and the offsets. |
| `__sub` | `(other: UDim): UDim` | Subtracts the scales and the offsets. |
| `__eq` | `(other: UDim): boolean` | Compares the scale and the offset exactly. |

## UDim2

A UI position or size on two axes: one `UDim` for X and one for Y. The `Position` and `Size` of every `UIObject` are `UDim2` values.

Returns a `UDim2` with the given offsets in pixels and zero scales, for a fixed size or position.

### `fromScale(xs: number? = 0, ys: number? = 0): UDim2`

Returns a `UDim2` with the given scales and zero offsets, for a size or position relative to the parent.

### `new(xs: number? = 0, xo: number? = 0, ys: number? = 0, yo: number? = 0): UDim2`

Returns a `UDim2` from four numbers: the X scale, the X offset, the Y scale and the Y offset.

|---|---|---|---|---|
| `X` | `UDim` | — | read-only | The `UDim` of the horizontal axis. |
| `Y` | `UDim` | — | read-only | The `UDim` of the vertical axis. |

## UDim2 — methods

### `Lerp(goal: UDim2, alpha: number): UDim2`

Returns the interpolation toward `goal`, with each of the four numbers interpolated independently. A tween of a `Position` or `Size` computes the same values.

## UDim2 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: UDim2): UDim2` | Adds both axes. |
| `__sub` | `(other: UDim2): UDim2` | Subtracts both axes. |

## Vector2

A vector of two 32-bit floats, used mostly for screen positions and sizes. It supports `+`, `-`, unary `-`, `*` and `/` by a number on either side or by another `Vector2` component by component, and an exact `==`.

## Vector2 — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The vector `(1, 1)`. |
| `zero` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The vector `(0, 0)`. |

## Vector2 — constructors

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0): Vector2`

Returns a vector with the given components. Each defaults to 0.

## Vector2 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Magnitude` | `number` | — | read-only | The length of the vector. |
| `Unit` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The vector scaled to a length of 1. The unit of a zero vector is the zero vector. |
| `X` | `number` | — | read-only | The horizontal component. It is uppercase, unlike `Vector3.x`. |
| `Y` | `number` | — | read-only | The vertical component. In screen coordinates, Y increases downward. |

## Vector2 — methods

### `Dot(other: Vector2): number`

Returns the dot product with another vector.

### `Lerp(goal: Vector2, alpha: number): Vector2`

Returns the linear interpolation toward `goal`. `alpha` is not clamped, so a value outside 0 to 1 extrapolates.

## Vector2 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Adds two vectors component by component. |
| `__sub` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Subtracts one vector from another component by component. |
| `__unm` | `(): Vector2` | Negates the vector. |
| `__mul` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Multiplies two vectors component by component. |
| `__mul` | `(scalar: number): Vector2` | Multiplies a vector by a number. The number can be on either side. |
| `__div` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Divides one vector by another component by component. |
| `__div` | `(scalar: number): Vector2` | Divides a vector by a number, or a number by a vector, component by component. |
| `__eq` | `(other: Vector2): boolean` | Compares two vectors exactly, component by component, with no tolerance. |

## Vector3

A vector of three 32-bit floats. It is Luau's native `vector` type, not an object: `typeof` returns `"vector"`, and arithmetic allocates no memory. Its components are the lowercase fields `x`, `y` and `z`.

The `Vector3` global is the `vector` library plus `new`, so every function is available under both names, and `Vector3.zero == vector.zero`.

The operators are `+`, `-` (binary and unary), `*` and `/` (by a number on either side, or by another vector component by component), `//`, `%` and `==`.

A 32-bit float is exact to the millimeter up to about 8 km from the origin, and to about 16 mm at 131 km. For positions in a very large world, work with `CFrame`, which stores its position in 64 bits.

## Vector3 — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one` | `vector` | — | read-only | The vector `(1, 1, 1)`. |
| `zero` | `vector` | — | read-only | The vector `(0, 0, 0)`. |

## Vector3 — constructors

### `abs(v: vector): vector`

Returns a vector with the absolute value of each component.

### `angle(a: vector, b: vector, axis: vector? = nil): number`

Returns the angle between two vectors, in radians, from 0 to π. With `axis`, the angle is signed about that axis by the right-hand rule and ranges from -π to π.

### `ceil(v: vector): vector`

Returns a vector with each component rounded up.

### `clamp(v: vector, min: vector, max: vector): vector`

Returns a vector with each component clamped between the matching components of `min` and `max`. Raises an error if a component of `min` is greater than that of `max`.

### `create(x: number, y: number, z: number? = 0): vector`

Returns a vector with the given components. It is the constructor of Luau's standard `vector` library, for code shared with other Luau runtimes. Unlike `new`, it requires `x` and `y`.

### `cross(a: vector, b: vector): vector`

Returns the cross product of two vectors. It is right-handed: for the axes of any `CFrame`, `cross(right, up) == -look`.

### `dot(a: vector, b: vector): number`

Returns the dot product of two vectors.

### `floor(v: vector): vector`

Returns a vector with each component rounded down.

### `lerp(a: vector, b: vector, alpha: number): vector`

Returns the linear interpolation from `a` to `b`, component by component. `alpha` is not clamped, so a value outside 0 to 1 extrapolates.

### `magnitude(v: vector): number`

Returns the length of a vector. It is faster than reading the `Magnitude` field.

### `max(a: vector, rest: ...vector): vector`

Returns a vector with the largest value of each component among the arguments. The result is the corner of their bounding box opposite the one `min` returns.

### `min(a: vector, rest: ...vector): vector`

Returns a vector with the smallest value of each component among the arguments. The result is a corner of their bounding box, not the shortest argument.

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0, z: number? = 0): vector`

Returns a vector with the given components. A missing component is 0. The call allocates no memory.

### `normalize(v: vector): vector`

Returns a vector scaled to a length of 1. Normalizing a zero vector returns NaN components; it does not raise an error.

### `sign(v: vector): vector`

Returns a vector with -1, 0 or 1 for each component, according to its sign.

## Vector3 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Magnitude` | `number` | — | read-only | The length of the vector. `vector.magnitude(v)` returns the same value and is faster. |
| `Unit` | `vector` | — | read-only | The vector scaled to a length of 1. `vector.normalize(v)` returns the same value and is faster. |
| `x` | `number` | — | read-only | The X component. The component names are lowercase because they are fields of Luau's native vector type. `v.X` also reads the component at run time, but only the lowercase name is declared, so the type checker rejects the uppercase one. |
| `y` | `number` | — | read-only | The Y component. Y is up. |
| `z` | `number` | — | read-only | The Z component. Forward is -Z, so a direction that points forward has a negative `z`. |

## Vector3 — methods

### `Angle(other: vector, axis: vector? = nil): number`

Returns the angle to `other`, in radians. It is the method form of `vector.angle`, including the optional `axis`.

### `Cross(other: vector): vector`

Returns the cross product with `other`, in that order. It is the method form of `vector.cross`. The order matters: `a:Cross(b) == -b:Cross(a)`.

### `Dot(other: vector): number`

Returns the dot product with `other`. It is the method form of `vector.dot`.

### `Lerp(goal: vector, alpha: number): vector`

Returns the linear interpolation toward `goal`. It is the method form of `vector.lerp`. `alpha` is not clamped.

## WorldStep

One tick of the world, passed to a function bound with `RunService:BindToWorldStep`. It is valid only during that call.

## WorldStep — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DeltaTime` | `number` | — | read-only | The length of the step, in seconds. |
| `Predicted` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether this machine is a client simulating a tick ahead of its authority. It is false on the authority and in a single-player game. |
| `Random` | `Random` | — | read-only | A random number generator seeded from `Tick`. It gives the same numbers on every machine and in every replay of the tick. Each read returns a generator at the start of its sequence, so store it in a local variable. |
| `Replaying` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether this step is being simulated again after a correction, on a client. Check it before doing something that must happen only once, such as playing a sound. |
| `Tick` | `number` | — | read-only | The authority's tick number for this step. On a client it is the tick at which the authority will simulate the tick being predicted, so a part placed from it is where the authority will have it. |
